query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC/BCC high‐entropy alloy multilayers, sustained loading causes progressive plastic deformation because dislocations, generated primarily in the FCC layers, accumulate and transfer at the coherent FCC/BCC interfaces. The severe lattice distortion inherent to HEAs then promotes dislocation core spreading and a transition from glide to climb-controlled deformation in the BCC layers.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanoscale multilayer coating composed of alternating, coherent FCC and BCC high‐entropy alloy layers with a controlled layer period and minimal initial dislocation density.
generation.intervention: Subject the multilayer coating to a constant, sustained uniaxial load under creep conditions at an intermediate temperature (where diffusion is active enough to enable dislocation climb).
generation.conditions: Creep tests under constant stress and controlled temperature, with additional controlled comparisons by varying layer thickness (altering interface density) and interface coherence.
generation.structural_mediator: The coherent FCC/BCC interfaces that act as strong dislocation barriers and sites for dislocation pile-up.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained loading, dislocations nucleate in the FCC layers and accumulate at the FCC/BCC interfaces. The severe lattice distortion in HEAs induces wavy dislocation lines that reduce effective glide mobility, thereby forcing accumulated dislocations to climb in the BCC layers. This switch from glide-dominated to climb-assisted creep drives the progressive plastic deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Over time, the material will exhibit an increasing strain rate accompanied by microstructural evidence (via TEM) of dislocation pile-ups at interfaces and signs of dislocation climb in the BCC layers. Additionally, reducing the layer thickness (thus, increasing the interface density) should lead to a more rapid onset of the climb-dominated deformation.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited nanoscale multilayer structure with intact coherent interfaces and low dislocation density, exhibiting primarily elastic behavior with minimal plastic activity.
generation.boundary: If the multilayer structure is altered such that the layers are too thick or the interfaces become incoherent (for example, due to processing variations), the interface-mediated barrier effect diminishes and the deformation behavior may revert to that of a homogeneous high-entropy alloy without the prominent transition from glide to climb.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative influence of lattice distortion and interface spacing on the transition from glide to climb remains uncertain and requires systematic experimental investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy multilayers with controlled variations in layer thickness (e.g., 10 nm, 50 nm, 100 nm) and interfacial coherence. Subject all samples to sustained uniaxial creep tests at an intermediate temperature. Use in-situ TEM or post-deformation TEM imaging to examine dislocation structures, particularly at the interfaces, and measure strain vs time curves.
measurements: Creep strain vs time to determine the strain rate evolution
TEM analysis of dislocation density and distribution at the interfaces
Activation energy estimates from the creep behavior
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If altering the layer thickness or interface coherence does not significantly affect the creep rate or fails to reveal increased dislocation accumulation and evidence of dislocation climb at the interfaces, then the proposed mechanism is not supported and must be falsified.

System: Nb23.8Ta25.5Ti24.9V25.8 (nominally Nb25Ta25Ti25V25) BCC refractory high-entropy alloy. System: Equiatomic FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy (Co-free variant of the Cantor alloy). Processing: Molecular dynamics simulations using LAMMPS software with Embedded-atom method (EAM) potential; model size 108.3 Å × 108.3 Å × 180.5 Å (180,000 atoms); relaxation via heating to 1000 K and cooling to 300 K; tensile loading at temperatures of 10 K, 300 K, 600 K and strain rates of 10^8 s^-1, 10^9 s^-1, 10^10 s^-1 along <110>, <1-12>, and <-111> orientations..
